doc.title: David Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 18, 2003

title: Finding your own sound by writing your own music
summary: Agreeing that young players sound alike, advice to write and rearrange your own pieces, and Ben Webster practicing baritone.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: That step of trying to go from learning all that material and then forming your own sound seems to be a big thing in the jazz community. I know like, especially talking to real veteran guys in their seventies and eighties, and they’ll listen to the current players. They seem to think that they’re cookie cutter, they’re all sounding the same.
They are sounding the same. And I think I agree with them. I think the reason is because they’ve got so much information and they don’t know how to — how do you say —

Edit all this information inside. You know they have to be able to get all these things in order to have certain techniques but they have to use that to get to who they are. They have to go inside. What kids have to do, they have to start writing music themselves. They have to learn. When I came to New York, the way I learned, I had learned a lot of bebop and all that before I got to New York. And so when I got to New York I kept studying. I’m always — I study bebop even now, just to keep sharp, just to read something. You get up in the morning and go through the Omni book. When you go back to the Omni book it takes you days to go through it. Now it takes me an hour to go through it. It’s like that. All those books are like that. You should be able to go through them in about 45 minutes after you do it every day. Then just throw it away for a while, just leave that one alone. You learn stuff to forget it. I don’t know if that makes any sense, but jazz musicians say that all the time.
You’re keeping the concepts, but not the actual lines.
Yeah. No, you don’t want to be somebody. You want to be who you are. And I really think like when I came to New York I started writing a lot. And I learned about myself © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

through, like I’ll do a piece like “Morning Song” or something like that, or any song. And next thing I do an octet arrangement, the next thing I do a big band arrangement of the same song. And so in that I’m learning about music through my song, through my own song. I suggest to most kids that they should write their own music and then put it through a couple of different keys and really start to understand what their music can teach them about themselves. Then they’re getting closer to finding out who they are. And in this process, playing your own stuff on the horn, playing for hours and hours of your own ideas, that’s when you start to get up there when the Ornette Colemans and the Birds and the Sonny Rollinses and the Clifford Jordans and all these people, that kind of time that you spend just working out your own personal ideas. That’s how you get a sound, by working like that. I mean like for instance I don’t know if a lot of people know it but Ben Webster you know, I met an old girlfriend of Ben Webster and she used to always tell me she’d say you know when Ben was living up here in Sccandinavia he used to only practice on baritone. He wouldn’t play the tenor until he came to the gig. There’s ways. That would get you a sound.
It’s like running with weights on your feet.
